description:
We are a team interested in science, technology, space exploration, and data analysis. Our goal is to develop interdisciplinary, science-based solutions to address environmental and technological challenges.

We welcome collaborators with knowledge or interests in agriculture, environmental science, programming, statistical analysis, and Geographic Information Systems (GIS).
summary:
Nexora-11 is an interactive, bilingual web platform that compares regions of the Moon and Mars with places on Earth that resemble them. Users explore 3D globes of the Moon, Mars, Phobos and Deimos. For each study region or mission site, including the lunar south pole and the Jezero and Gale landing sites, the platform shows its estimated local conditions and ranks the most similar Earth analogs, with live weather and climate data from NASA POWER and Open-Meteo.

It addresses the challenge by characterizing analogs, not just listing them. A traceable database of 17 sites and 26 parameters supports a similarity model across climate, hydrology, geology and radiation that shows how similar a site is, by how much, and where the analogy ends. The team also proposes three analogs not found on NASA or ESA lists: Poás and Rincón de la Vieja volcanoes in Costa Rica, and Lake Salda in Turkey.

This matters because choosing the right test sites reduces mission risks.
details:
Nexora-11 is an interactive, bilingual (English/Spanish) web platform that compares regions of the Moon and Mars with places on Earth that resemble them. Users explore 3D globes of the Moon and Mars, including Phobos and Deimos, and select one of 10 study regions or 14 historic mission sites, such as the lunar south pole (a candidate area for permanent Artemis bases) and the Jezero and Gale landing sites. They can also click any point on the surface.

For each selection, the platform shows the body’s fixed data and the estimated local conditions of that point: local solar time, temperature, pressure, radiation, soil composition, geology and hydrology. It then ranks the most similar Earth analogs. For each analog it shows a real photo with its author and license, plus live weather and climate data from Open-Meteo and NASA POWER.

Behind the interface is a traceable scientific database of 17 sites and 26 parameters grouped into four domains (climate, hydrology, geology and radiation). Every value records its source, unit, method, uncertainty and type of evidence. A weighted similarity model (geology 35%, climate 30%, hydrology 20%, radiation 15%) only produces a result when coverage reaches at least 70% and 8 variables. In the current prototype, the similarity bars are illustrative and are labeled as such on screen, because the database values are still being loaded.

Benefits and intended impact

No place on Earth is identical to another world, and choosing the wrong test site increases mission risks. Nexora-11 shows how similar a site is, by how much, and where the analogy ends. It also brings together information that is currently scattered across papers, mission archives and databases. Agencies and researchers can use it to choose where to test rovers, suits and instruments. Teachers and students can use it to explore the Moon and Mars and understand what makes them different from Earth.

Creativity

Beyond the well-known analogs, the team researched and proposed three that are not on NASA or ESA analog lists. The first is Poás volcano in Costa Rica, whose crater lake has a pH between −0.87 and 1.5 and resembles the acid-sulfate hydrothermal systems of ancient Mars. The second is Rincón de la Vieja volcano, with an equally acidic crater lake; we found no studies using it as a Mars analog. The third is Lake Salda in Turkey, the only known lake with carbonates and deltas similar to those of Jezero crater. The platform highlights these proposals on the Earth globe.

Tools and technologies

The site uses HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with Three.js (r128) for the 3D rendering. Data comes from the NASA POWER and Open-Meteo APIs and the Wikimedia Commons API, plus NASA Planetary Fact Sheets and PDS mission data as reference values. The scientific database is stored in JSON and CSV. The textures come from Solar System Scope (CC BY 4.0). It is a static site with no server or database of its own and runs in any modern browser. Claude (Anthropic) was used as an SI assistant for code development, and the demo video’s voice-over was generated with Kokoro TTS. Both are disclosed in the project.

Factors the team considered

Scientific honesty was the guiding principle. The site always states whether a value is fixed, estimated, illustrative or real-time. The team also considered data traceability, accessibility (bilingual, no installation needed), the fact that no analog is complete (gravity, vacuum and cosmic radiation cannot be reproduced on Earth), and a path to scale the analysis through three levels of characterization: public satellite data, high-resolution remote sensing with drones or LiDAR, and fieldwork.
